text: Amédée (Aimé) Gibaud (5 March 1885 – 18 August 1957), born and died in Rochefort-sur-Mer, was a French chess master. He won the French Chess Championship four times, in 1928, 1930, 1935, and 1940, and secured the French correspondence championship three times, in 1929, 1931, and 1932. He tied for fourth/fifth at the Ramsgate 1929 tournament (Premier A), where William Gibson emerged as the winner. Gibaud represented France in the first unofficial Chess Olympiad held in Paris in 1924 and in the third unofficial Chess Olympiad in Munich in 1936. A brief miniature chess game attributed to Gibaud and Frédéric Lazard is frequently reproduced in chess literature, sometimes claimed to be the shortest game ever played between masters in a formal setting. In its most commonly cited version, the game consists of four moves by each player, with Black (Lazard) rapidly developing the king's knight to e3 after White (Gibaud) weakens the defense of the square. In the final position, White cannot prevent the capture of his queen, as 5. fxe3 Qh4+ leads to 6. g3 Qxg3#. The four-move, "formal" version of this game is not recognized as a real historical event. Gibaud denied ever losing a serious game in four moves, stating instead that he may have lost a casual skittles game against Lazard with similar positional ideas, involving more than four moves. He also suggested that his game with Lazard might have been confused with a previously published "theoretical" miniature. Although the four-move version is not considered historically accurate, it demonstrates key gameplay principles: the risks of rapid development, the importance of not weakening defenses of critical squares, and the necessity of guarding structural weaknesses on the kingside—particularly involving the f- and g-pawns—during the opening phase, as unguarded weaknesses can lead to quick checkmate, similar to Fool's mate.
